name: LeanyLabs assemblyscript-benchmarks (factorial)
baseline: JavaScript (recursive factorial) in V8 under Node
workload: Six micro-benchmarks run with benchmark.js: add (boundary crossing), factorial(20), squareArray, calcSinLookup, importCallback and averageIfLess over 2 million float64 values.
claimed_speedup: factorial: AssemblyScript 14,076,129 ops/sec vs JavaScript 6,483,418 ops/sec (2.17x, derived from page data). calcSinLookup tied (11,450 vs 11,417 ops/sec). JavaScript wins the other four: add 697M vs 126M, squareArray 822k vs 432k, importCallback 352k vs 24k, averageIfLess 338 vs 294 ops/sec.
compiler_and_flags: asc (assemblyscript ^0.18.4) release target in asconfig.json: optimizeLevel 3, shrinkLevel 0, converge, noAssert; benchmark.js 2.1.4; Node version not stated
hardware: Intel Core i5-8250 (as written in the README), 16 GB RAM, Ubuntu 20.04 LTS
tradeoffs: AssemblyScript pays for every JS/Wasm boundary crossing: passing arrays and calling imports is 2-15x slower than plain JavaScript, so only compute-heavy code with small arguments wins.
caveats: Mixed result: AssemblyScript wins one of six workloads, ties one and loses four, so this is evidence of a narrow win (and of boundary cost), not a general speedup; 2021 numbers on AssemblyScript 0.18 and an unnamed Node version; the recursive factorial(20) is a tiny kernel and the two sides do not compute the same thing: the AssemblyScript version is i32 (assembly/index.ts: factorial(i: i32): i32), so 20! wraps around, while the JavaScript version returns the exact float64 value; the harness does not check results.
found_via: GitHub: web search 'AssemblyScript vs JavaScript benchmark github repository results' (result list)

verification.tier_reason: Code (benchmarks.js, assembly/index.ts), asc 0.18.4 with -O3 release flags (asconfig.json, package-lock.json) and the i5-8250 CPU are public, but the Node/V8 version that JIT-compiles both sides is not stated, and the one winning row compares different computations, so no valid number shows AssemblyScript faster.
verification.notes: Numbers match the README exactly. Reject on the stb-zip/fast_resize precedent: the factorial win comes from wrapping i32 arithmetic that returns a wrong value, compared against JavaScript computing the right one. Otherwise JavaScript wins 4 of 6 and ties 1. If the orchestrator prefers to keep it, record it as a duplicate of the wave-12 AssemblyScript entry, which already cites this repo.
verification.reject_reason: other: wrong-answer fast path and known project. The only row AssemblyScript wins (factorial) compares an i32 AssemblyScript factorial that overflows at 20 (returns -2102132736) against a JavaScript factorial that computes the exact 20! in float64; every row that computes the same thing shows AssemblyScript slower or tied. The page is also an evidence page for AssemblyScript (https://github.com/assemblyscript/assemblyscript, wave 12, tier D), whose caveats already cite these LeanyLabs results.

name: SIMDMatrixAlgorithm
language: x86-64 NASM assembly with C and C++ drivers
baseline: scalar C and scalar C++ matrix multiply compiled with gcc -O3
claimed_speedup: README table: scalar C ~0.6 s (<1 GFLOP/s); scalar C++ ~1.3 s; NASM XMM (SSE, 2x unroll) ~0.29 s (~10 GFLOP/s); NASM YMM (AVX, 4x unroll) ~0.0098 s (~28 GFLOP/s), about 60x versus scalar C (derived); hybrid C+ASM and C++ +ASM ~0.010 to 0.020 s.
tradeoffs: x86-64 AVX/FMA only; fixed unrolling; single-precision square matrices.
caveats: Gap above 50x, so tier capped at C: the baseline is a naive scalar triple loop that stays unvectorized and uncached despite -O3 -mavx -mfma, so the gap reflects missing blocking and vectorization in the baseline, not asm versus well-optimized compiler output. GFLOP/s and CPI columns have no methodology. README mentions AVX-512 gains of about 30x with no zmm build or data (and the Ryzen 5 5600X has no AVX-512).
found_via: WebSearch 'github README hand-written assembly implementation benchmark table versus portable C compiled with gcc -O3'

verification.tier_reason: The README table does compare scalar C/C++ with the NASM XMM/YMM and hybrid kernels on a named CPU (Ryzen 5 5600X) with stated gcc flags. However, the timed kernels produce wrong results, there is no correctness check, and the table contradicts itself, so the numbers carry no usable evidence. If the entry is kept, list it as D.
verification.notes: Reject per the stb-zip and fast_resize precedents (the fast path computes a different result): every timed asm path miscomputes the product (wrong M2 stride, lane-dropping horizontal add, results never stored, overlapping hybrid loads), and the README table contradicts itself (XMM 0.29 s labelled ~10 GFLOP/s; an AVX-512 claim with no zmm code on a Zen 3 CPU). If the orchestrator prefers keep-and-document, keep it at D with these shortcomings: 0-star student project, MIT, last commit 2025-10-14 (active).
verification.reject_reason: Invalid evidence: the measured kernels compute wrong answers (M2 rows read 1952 bytes apart instead of 2048, vhaddps drops the upper 128-bit lane, NASM results are never stored, the hybrid C ymm loads overlap at 16-byte offsets); the table contradicts itself (XMM 0.29 s labelled about 10 GFLOP/s; an AVX-512 30x claim with no zmm code on a Zen 3); the C++ baseline is double and copied by value. stb-zip and fast_resize precedent.

name: @unconfirmed/bcs (bcs-zig WebAssembly)
workload: BCS serialize plus deserialize round trips of structs, enums, u64/u128/u256, vectors and addresses, 300K iterations on Bun.
claimed_speedup: 5.2x average; SimpleStruct (41 B) 10.7M vs 1.3M ops/s (7.9x), Option<Struct> 7.7M vs 921K (8.3x), Vec<u32> (1000) 410K vs 91K (4.5x); raw serializeInto() about 10x+ faster serialization
tradeoffs: Drop-in API for @mysten/bcs but needs a wasm runtime; the raw entry point requires manual buffer management.
caveats: Numbers measured on Bun with no hardware stated and no benchmark folder in the repo (README only). A live browser benchmark is linked but was not opened. First-party; very young project.
found_via: npm registry search (query 'webassembly simd') then github.com/unconfirmedlabs/bcs README Benchmarks section

verification.tier_reason: First-party README tables (roundtrip vs @mysten/bcs, 300K iterations on Bun; raw serializeInto vs @mysten serialize) with no benchmark code in the repo (src/ and test/ hold only bcs.test.ts and compat.test.ts), no @mysten/bcs version, Bun version or CPU stated; the linked live benchmark bcs-benchmark.vercel.app does not resolve (ENOTFOUND).
verification.notes: Numbers match the README, but the record's framing is wrong: the Zig/WASM module is bundled and exported (loadWasm) yet unused on every measured path, so this is a pure TypeScript runtime-codegen serializer beating another JS serializer. Recommend override name '@unconfirmed/bcs', language 'TypeScript (runtime codegen via new Function)', and either keep in wasm-libraries-and-apps with the shortcoming 'WASM not on measured path' or move to a JS serialization category; second shortcoming: no public harness, live benchmark host dead.
verification.reject_reason: Invalid evidence for the catalogued claim: the measured speedup comes from pure TypeScript new Function() codegen and the bcs-zig WebAssembly build is never called on the measured paths (src/wasm.ts says so), so the numbers do not measure the WebAssembly implementation the record claims (Go stdlib libp2p 'OpenSSL' precedent). Also: no harness in the repo, the live benchmark host is unreachable, the table's 'Average 5.2x' contradicts its own rows (mean 6.5x), and the raw serializeInto table skips validation. Verifier batch-83.
